title: Ken Paxton’s Security for Travel Cost Taxpayers Millions. Just 1 in 6 of His Trips Had a Stated Business Purpose.
author: Zach Despart
content:
In the summer of 2023, after he was impeached on charges of abusing his office
for personal gain, [Texas Attorney General Ken
Paxton](https://directory.texastribune.org/ken-paxton/) was suspended and
barred from conducting any official business for more than three months while
awaiting trial in the state Senate.

So, he traveled.

Paxton, a Republican who is now running for U.S. Senate, took at least 17
trips over three months, including to resort destinations Park City, Utah, and
Vail, Colorado. He visited the Oklahoma town where he owns a vacation lodge
and a Utah community with a golf resort, where he later bought four
condominiums.

State police joined him each time, costing taxpayers tens of thousands of
dollars for trips unrelated to his job as attorney general. The Texas Senate
ultimately acquitted him on the impeachment charges.

But Paxton’s use of the taxpayer-funded detail did not begin or end there. In
fact, it stands out compared with his predecessor, fellow elected officials in
Texas and other state attorneys general, ProPublica and The Texas Tribune
found.

Paxton has traveled frequently out of state while listing little on his
official calendar, The Associated Press [reported last
week](https://apnews.com/article/ken-paxton-travel-expenses-campaign-texas-
talarico-dba14655a17ab0cc4a82f76d4faecd28). ProPublica and the Tribune’s
analysis, which included reviewing every publicly available document Paxton’s
office says it possesses about his travel, discloses for the first time how
few of his trips had a listed business purpose: just 1 in 6.

It also found Paxton’s security has cost taxpayers far more than has
previously been reported.

Since assuming office in 2015, Paxton has taken nearly 1,000 trips with a
state-funded security detail, costing $3.3 million. The newsrooms’ review of
Paxton’s travel records, obtained through the state’s Public Information Act,
could only connect 138 of those trips and $553,000 in security costs to state
business.

Records detailing the purpose of Paxton’s visits to 36 states and 19 countries
do not appear to exist in most cases. These include a trip to a small town in
Hawaii months before his family’s blind trust bought land there; 24 trips to
Utah, where the trust owns five properties; and 53 trips to Florida, where
Paxton and the trust have two houses and a townhome.

“If you’ve got all these extra trips, it becomes ethically and morally
problematic,” said Chris Toth, former executive director of the National
Association of Attorneys General, who has also criticized Paxton’s conduct on
other issues. “The ethical question is whether a legitimate security function
has effectively become a taxpayer-funded subsidy.”

Texas law allows the Department of Public Safety to provide security for key
state leaders, including the attorney general, but does not require officials
to use it. In fact, Paxton himself hasn’t used it in at least two dozen cases
while traveling on official business.

Paxton has dismissed opponents’ attacks that he has used the perks of office
to benefit himself and has not answered questions about how he [vastly
increased his wealth](https://www.propublica.org/article/ken-paxton-senate-
financial-disclosures-ethics-law) as a public servant.

He also did not answer detailed questions for this story. ProPublica and the
Tribune sent Paxton a spreadsheet detailing travel for which there was no
record that he was on state business and asked him to provide additional
information if the trips were not personal. Neither Paxton nor his office
provided such records. Instead, his office provided a general statement.

“Throughout his career, Ken Paxton has faced numerous security threats
stemming from his courageous work as Attorney General fighting on behalf of
the people of Texas,” his office said in the statement. “Those threats are a
direct result of him taking on the cartels terrorizing Texans and some of the
nation’s most dangerous violent criminals.”

Paxton’s office directed additional questions to DPS.

A DPS spokesperson declined to answer the newsrooms’ questions, saying the
agency does not comment on its security arrangements.

![A document showing a Texas Department of Public Safety expense report
listing out-of-state and in-state executive protection travel costs for the
attorney general in the fourth quarter of fiscal year
2023.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/PaxtonTravelv2_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Logs
from the Texas Department of Public Safety security detail assigned to
Attorney General Ken Paxton show multiple out-of-state trips while he was
suspended from office in 2023. Obtained and highlighted by ProPublica and The
Texas Tribune

### An Outlier Among Peers

To analyze Paxton’s travel, ProPublica and the Tribune reviewed DPS logs for
his security detail and records from the attorney general’s office, including
airfare and lodging receipts, per diems and his daily calendars.

The records available for his predecessor, [Greg
Abbott](https://directory.texastribune.org/greg-abbott/), show a stark
difference: Abbott traveled mostly within the state as attorney general, and
his security cost $203,000 during his last three years in the office. Adjusted
for inflation, Abbott’s security detail cost $7,400 per month. Paxton’s has
averaged $24,300.

Because the state keeps records only for a limited time, Abbott’s travel
expenses and his daily calendars as attorney general no longer exist, so the
news organizations could not determine how many of his trips were for
business.

Records are available, however, for Abbott’s security costs as governor and
for [Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick](https://directory.texastribune.org/dan-patrick/).
Both are also offered state police security and have been in their current
roles as long as Paxton.

When compared, the records show Paxton has taken 82 more out-of-state trips
with a security detail than Abbott and nearly as many as the governor and
lieutenant governor combined.

Though DPS security detail records are available for state leaders’ full
tenure, Abbott’s office only provided calendars that document business-related
activity for his first six years in office. More than two-thirds of the
governor’s international trips during those years had a listed business
purpose, compared with just two of 25 for Paxton during his full tenure. The
governor’s office said it planned to release the remaining five years on
Tuesday but only provided five months, saying it needed more time.

The attorney general’s records do not show a business purpose for travel to
Albania, Aruba, Australia, Costa Rica, the Czech Republic, the Dominican
Republic, England, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Malta, Mexico,
Poland, South Africa or Taiwan.

The share of Paxton’s travel with a documented business purpose peaked early
in his tenure, in 2018 and 2019, at 30%, the newsrooms’ analysis found. That
aligns with the governor’s share of business travel during that period.

Since then, Paxton has taken fewer trips that are documented as state business
while increasingly traveling out of state. Last year, just five of Paxton’s 91
trips with the security detail had a listed business purpose. Forty-one were
outside Texas.

In some cases, Paxton has taken business trips without a DPS detail, an
analysis of records from the department and the attorney general’s office
shows. They include a 2019 meeting in Nashville, Tennessee, with that state’s
attorney general to discuss opioid litigation and a 2021 visit with unnamed
U.S. senators in North Carolina. There is also no record of Paxton taking the
detail on political fundraising trips to Florida and the Bahamas.

But Paxton has traveled with security to other campaign-related activities,
including one that came just two days after he was acquitted in the
impeachment trial. Paxton boarded a Maine-bound private plane owned by a North
Texas businessman to tape an episode of Tucker Carlson’s show, according to
campaign finance records. During the interview, he hinted that he’d challenge
U.S. Sen. John Cornyn in the 2026 Republican primary.

“Everything is on the table for me,” Paxton said when Carlson suggested he
should run.

In his interview with Carlson, Paxton said it was unfair that he was
automatically suspended before he could clear his name. He said he was eager
to get back to work and that he was “reenergized to do the things the voters
sent me to do.”

Paxton should pay for his own security on trips where there is no benefit for
Texans, like vacations and campaign events, said Richard Briffault, a
professor at Columbia Law School who has written about government ethics.

“There’s no reason for the taxpayers to be paying for things that they would
not be paying for if he had stayed home,” Briffault said. “That’s a misuse of
public funds.”

State officials said there are no records of Paxton or his campaign
reimbursing Texas for security costs.

Of the 10 most populous states, Texas and New York confirmed that they provide
security for their attorneys general, while Florida law allows its top lawyer
to receive a detail upon request. North Carolina does not. Attorneys general
offices for the remaining six states did not respond to requests for comment.

Former Oregon Attorney General Ellen Rosenblum said she never used a security
detail during her 12 years in office, which ended in 2024. The Democrat said
that Paxton’s higher profile might create a greater need for protection, but
his extensive out-of-state travel without a documented business purpose raises
questions about his workload.

“Was he minding the store? There’s a lot of work to be done at the office,”
Rosenblum said.

### Travel and Real Estate

Some of Paxton’s travel to four states with a security detail has overlapped
with locations where he or his family’s trust has purchased 10 properties
since 2021. A recent [ProPublica and Tribune
analysis](https://www.propublica.org/article/ken-paxton-senate-financial-
disclosures-ethics-law) found he owns or co-owns 15 properties with a market
value of about $11 million.

In June 2021, Paxton attended an attorneys general conference in Maui. The
security detail listed the destination as Lahaina, a small community on the
Hawaiian island’s west coast. Four months later, Paxton’s family trust
purchased an oceanview lot in a residential neighborhood there for $410,000,
land records show.

The 7,000-square-foot lot remains vacant but has proved to be a savvy
investment, now assessed at $1.2 million by Maui County.

Paxton set up the trust with his estranged wife, [State Sen. Angela
Paxton](https://directory.texastribune.org/angela-paxton/), who declined to be
interviewed but said through a spokesperson that she has not been involved in
her husband’s business dealings since 2024, when she filed for divorce. The
Paxtons’ friend, Chip Loper, runs the trust. He did not respond to requests
for comment.

Paxton has also gone to the Salt Lake City area 19 times, twice for listed
business purposes. He visited three times — once on business — in the months
leading up to his family trust’s July 2021 purchase of a plot in the ski town
of Eden. The trust bought a mountainside lot on about two-thirds of an acre
for $315,000 in cash, the seller told the newsrooms. It also remains
undeveloped.

During his suspension in August 2023, Paxton visited St. George, Utah, a small
city in the state’s southwest corner. Nearby is the Black Desert Resort, which
hosts an annual PGA Tour golf tournament. Paxton purchased one condo at the
resort in 2025 and three more in February. Paxton took out mortgages totaling
$1.9 million for them, according to legal documents filed with the local
county.

Paxton has visited Florida more than any other state, 53 times. Two of those
trips have a documented business purpose. Between 2021 and 2022, Paxton
purchased two homes in Ocala, known for its horse breeding industry, and a
townhome in Dunedin, on the Gulf of Mexico near Tampa.

Paxton also traveled with the detail twice to Broken Bow, Oklahoma, where he
purchased a $1.5 million vacation lodge in 2022. He visited in June 2023,
during his suspension. Then again the following December. He traveled to the
neighboring town of Idabel in 2023 and 2024. None of the trips had a listed
business purpose.

Records that show travel with a security detail do not list the attorney
general’s name but rather the position. State officials familiar with the
travel records said the two temporary attorneys general appointed during
Paxton’s suspension did not take the trips listed on the state police travel
logs.

The attorney general’s office has said that Paxton’s work to [secure large
legal settlements](https://www.propublica.org/article/ken-paxton-private-
lawyers-texas-cases) with drugmakers and tech companies requires routine
travel. Such travel is noted in calendars reviewed by ProPublica and the
Tribune. Even so, more than 800 trips lack a documented business purpose.

Paul Nolette, a Marquette University political science professor who studies
attorneys general, said that the role has become more expansive in recent
years as states increasingly collaborate on big lawsuits. That could lead to
more travel, he said. Nolette added these officials deserve occasional
vacations like everyday Americans.

But given repeated accusations from Democrats [and Republicans
alike](https://www.texastribune.org/2022/05/19/john-cornyn-ken-paxton-texas-
attorney-general-runoff/) about Paxton’s ethics, Nolette said it is difficult
to give him the benefit of the doubt that he’s constantly working while
leaving the state so frequently.

“It just raises more red flags about how he’s using the office to do things
that may not give the best bang for the buck for Texans,” Nolette said.

Paxton has not commented publicly about his use of the taxpayer-funded detail.
During a podcast interview in November, Houston lawyer Tony Buzbee, who led
his impeachment defense, asked the attorney general where he liked to travel.

“I love Jackson Hole. I like Park City. I like the mountains. I also like
beaches,” Paxton responded. “I like places in Florida, places in California,
even though I don’t like to admit I go to California. But it’s beautiful to
see them.”

The post [Ken Paxton’s Security for Travel Cost Taxpayers Millions. Just 1 in
6 of His Trips Had a Stated Business
Purpose.](https://www.propublica.org/article/ken-paxton-travel-security-costs)
appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
